chapters.title: The Branches of Biology and the Scientific Method

lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
Key Facts

  • Statements about the working of organs — the heart pumping blood, the stomach digesting food and the kidneys excreting wastes — belong to physiology, the study of the functions of living things.
  • In the scientific method, deductions are made from the hypothesis before experiments are performed: the scientist works out what should happen if the hypothesis is true.
  • It is NOT true that a hypothesis will always be correct: the scientific method relies on evidence, formulates hypotheses and tests them rigorously, and a hypothesis may be rejected.
  • The correct sequence of the steps of the scientific method is: observations → hypothesis → deduction → experiments.
  • People who slept near a smoky fire suffered less from malaria because mosquitoes cannot tolerate smoke and are repelled by it.
  • Experiments are important in the scientific method because through them a researcher disproves many hypotheses and gets some hypothesis proved.

mcqs.q: Statements about the working of organs — the heart pumping blood, the stomach digesting food and the kidneys excreting wastes — belong to which branch of biology?
mcqs.why: Physiology is the study of the functions of living things, and these statements describe how organs work, not what they look like.

mcqs.q: In the scientific method, deductions are made from the hypothesis at which stage?
options: Only after the conclusion is drawn
mcqs.why: The scientist first works out what should happen if the hypothesis is true; these deductions are made before experiments are performed to test them.

mcqs.q: Which statement about a hypothesis is correct?
options: A hypothesis may be rejected after testing
A hypothesis is already a proven law
mcqs.why: The scientific method relies on evidence and tests hypotheses rigorously, so a hypothesis that is not supported may be rejected.

mcqs.q: What is the correct sequence of steps in the scientific method?
mcqs.why: The correct sequence is observations first, then hypothesis, then deduction, and finally experiments to test the deductions.

mcqs.q: Why did people who slept near a smoky fire suffer less from malaria?
options: Mosquitoes cannot tolerate smoke and are repelled by it
Smoke kills the malaria parasite in the blood
Smoke makes the blood taste bitter
The fire raises the body temperature of sleepers
mcqs.why: Mosquitoes cannot tolerate smoke and are repelled by it, so people near smoky fires were bitten less and suffered less from malaria.

mcqs.q: Experiments are important in the scientific method because through them a researcher:
options: Disproves many hypotheses and gets some hypothesis proved
mcqs.why: Through experiments a researcher disproves many hypotheses and gets some hypothesis proved, which is how the correct explanation is found.

mcqs.q: The study of the functions of living things is called:
mcqs.why: Physiology is defined as the study of the functions of living things, such as how the heart pumps blood or the stomach digests food.

mcqs.q: A deduction in the scientific method states:
options: The final conclusion of the research
The result already obtained from experiments
What should happen if the hypothesis is true
mcqs.why: A deduction is the scientist working out what should happen if the hypothesis is true, so that experiments can be designed to test it.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a function studied in physiology?
options: The fossil record of a species
The classification of animals into groups
mcqs.why: Excreting wastes is a function performed by a living organ, so it belongs to physiology, the study of the functions of living things.

mcqs.q: If experimental results do not support a hypothesis, the hypothesis is:
options: Published as a theory at once
mcqs.why: The scientific method tests hypotheses rigorously against evidence, and it is not true that a hypothesis will always be correct — it may be rejected.

lessons.title: Short Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Branches of Biology: Genetics, Anatomy, Palaeontology, Marine Biology and Pathology

Genetics is the study of heredity and variation, that is, how characters pass from parents to offspring. Anatomy is the study of the internal structure of organisms. Palaeontology is the study of fossils and ancient life.

Marine Biology is the study of organisms living in the sea. Pathology is the study of diseases, their causes and effects on the body.

Morphology and Physiology

Morphology is the study of the form and external structure of organisms, such as the shape of leaves or the body plan of an animal. Physiology is the study of the functions of living things, such as how the heart pumps blood or how the stomach digests food. In short, morphology describes what an organism looks like, while physiology explains how it works.

Computational Biology

Computational Biology is the branch of biology in which computers, mathematics and statistics are used to study biological data. It is used to analyse large sets of data such as DNA sequences, to model living processes and to predict how biological systems behave. It helps biologists handle data too large to study by hand.

Observation and Experimentation in the Scientific Method

Observation is the starting point: a scientist notices a problem or a pattern in nature and gathers facts about it, and from these observations a hypothesis is formed. Experimentation tests the hypothesis under controlled conditions, so that deductions drawn from it can be checked. If the results agree with the deductions, the hypothesis is supported; if not, it is rejected or changed.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Biology and the Professions

Biology is the foundation of many professions. Medicine, dentistry, nursing and pharmacy all rest on knowledge of the human body, diseases and drugs. Agriculture, horticulture and veterinary science apply biology to crops and animals.

Other careers include biotechnology, food technology, fisheries, forestry and environmental science, where biological knowledge is used to improve health, food production and the environment.

From Hypothesis to Theory, Law and Principle

A hypothesis is a testable statement proposed to explain observations. When it is repeatedly tested by experiments and supported by evidence, it may become a theory, which is a well-tested explanation of a broad set of facts. A law or principle is a statement that describes a regular pattern in nature, such as what always happens under given conditions.

A theory explains why things happen, while a law describes what happens; neither is simply a guess.

Steps in Solving a Scientific Problem

The scientist first makes observations and identifies a problem, then collects information about it. Next a hypothesis is proposed to explain the problem, and deductions are drawn from the hypothesis, that is, what should happen if it is true. Experiments are then performed to test these deductions, results are analysed, and a conclusion is drawn.

If the results support the hypothesis it is accepted, otherwise it is modified and tested again.

Discovering the Cause of Malaria

Laveran (1880) first found the parasite Plasmodium in the blood of malaria patients. Manson suggested that mosquitoes carry the disease from person to person. Ronald Ross then showed, by experiments on birds and mosquitoes, that the parasite develops inside the mosquito and is passed on when the mosquito bites.

Later workers, including Grassi, confirmed that the female Anopheles mosquito transmits human malaria.

The Experiments of Ronald Ross

Ross studied malaria in birds, which is similar to human malaria. He allowed mosquitoes to feed on malaria-infected birds and then examined the stomach walls of the mosquitoes, where he found the developing parasites. He then showed that healthy birds bitten by such mosquitoes developed malaria.

This proved that mosquitoes are the carriers of malaria, and his work was later confirmed for human malaria in the Anopheles mosquito.

lessons.notes_html:
Biodiversity: The Variety of Life

The term is biodiversity. It means the variety of all living organisms, including different species, their genetic differences and the ecosystems in which they live.

Importance of Biodiversity for Humans and the Earth

Biodiversity keeps ecosystems stable and healthy: plants produce oxygen and food, decomposers recycle nutrients, and many species control pests and pollinate crops. For humans it provides food, medicines, timber and clean air and water. Loss of biodiversity weakens ecosystems and threatens human survival.

The Seven Taxonomic Ranks

From broadest to narrowest they are: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species. In the modern three-domain system, domain stands above kingdom as the broadest rank.

Archaea and Bacteria

Both are single-celled prokaryotes without a nucleus, but they differ in their cell walls and chemistry. Archaeal cell walls lack peptidoglycan, which bacterial walls contain, and archaeal cell membranes and genes are different. Archaea often live in extreme environments such as hot springs and salty lakes, while bacteria live almost everywhere.

Kingdom Animalia

Kingdom Animalia. Animals are multicellular, they obtain food by eating other organisms (heterotrophic nutrition), and their cells have no cell walls.

Distinguishing Characteristics of Fungi

Fungi are eukaryotic and mostly multicellular, with cell walls made of chitin. They are heterotrophic and absorb food from dead or living organic matter rather than making it. Their bodies are made of thread-like hyphae, and they reproduce by spores.

The Three Domains of Life

The three domains are Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya. Archaea and Bacteria contain prokaryotic organisms, while Eukarya contains all organisms with eukaryotic cells: protists, fungi, plants and animals.

Why Viruses Cannot Be Classified in Any Kingdom

Viruses are not cells: they have no cell membrane, cytoplasm or organelles, and they cannot carry out life processes on their own. They only reproduce inside a living host cell. Because the kingdom system classifies cellular living organisms, viruses fit into none of its kingdoms.

Binomial Nomenclature and Clear Communication

Binomial nomenclature gives every species one unique two-part Latin scientific name, a genus name followed by a species name, for example Homo sapiens. Because the same name is used by scientists in all countries, there is no confusion caused by different local or common names in different languages.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Biodiversity and the Health of Ecosystems

Biodiversity is the variety of genes, species and ecosystems on Earth. A diverse ecosystem is more stable because different species fill different roles: producers make food, consumers transfer energy, and decomposers return nutrients to the soil. If one species declines, others can partly take its place.

Biodiversity also gives humans food, medicines and raw materials, and protects soil, water and air, so its loss makes ecosystems fragile and less able to recover from change.

Importance of Classification in Biology

Classification groups organisms by shared characteristics into ranks from domain to species, so that the huge variety of life can be studied in an orderly way. Organisms placed in the same group share a common ancestry and similar features, so classification reveals evolutionary relationships. It also makes identification easy and allows scientists everywhere to communicate about the same organism without confusion.

Domains Archaea and Bacteria Compared

Both domains contain unicellular prokaryotes with no true nucleus or membrane-bound organelles, and both reproduce mainly by binary fission. They differ in cell wall chemistry: bacterial walls contain peptidoglycan, archaeal walls do not. Their membrane lipids and ribosomal RNA are also different, and archaea are famous for living in extreme conditions such as high temperature, high salt and acidity, while bacteria are found in almost every habitat.

The Four Kingdoms of Eukarya

Protista contains mostly unicellular eukaryotes, some with plant-like and some with animal-like nutrition. Fungi are heterotrophic eukaryotes with chitin cell walls that absorb food, and their bodies are made of hyphae. Plantae are multicellular, autotrophic eukaryotes with cellulose cell walls that make food by photosynthesis.

Animalia are multicellular, heterotrophic eukaryotes whose cells lack cell walls and which ingest their food.

Challenges of Classifying Viruses

The three-domain system classifies cellular life, but viruses are acellular particles made only of genetic material in a protein coat. They show no metabolism, growth or independent reproduction, and they are inactive outside a host cell. Some scientists regard them as non-living, others as living only inside a host.

Because they share features of both, and have no ribosomes or cell structure to compare, they cannot be placed in any domain or kingdom.

Rules for Scientific Names

As printed in the chapter (book p. 29): every scientific name has two parts, the genus name first followed by the species name. Each name must be unique, so the same name cannot be used for two different organisms.

The genus name begins with a capital letter and the species name with a small letter. In print the name is typed in italics, and when handwritten the two parts are underlined separately.

lessons.title: Short Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Functions of the Cell Membrane

The cell membrane separates the cell from its surroundings and protects its contents. It controls which substances enter and leave the cell, so it is selectively permeable. It also helps the cell communicate with its environment and gives the cell its shape.

Role of the Golgi Apparatus

The Golgi apparatus receives proteins and lipids from the endoplasmic reticulum, modifies them, packs them into vesicles and sends them to their destinations inside or outside the cell. It is therefore the packaging and dispatch centre of the cell.

How Lysosomes Serve the Cell

Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes that break down waste materials, worn-out organelles and foreign particles entering the cell. This cleaning and recycling keeps the cell healthy and supplies it with useful breakdown products.

The Organelle That Detoxifies: Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum

The smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER). It has no ribosomes on its surface and it synthesises lipids, detoxifies drugs and poisons, and breaks down lipids in the cell.

Functions of the Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum

The SER synthesises lipids and steroids, detoxifies harmful substances, and stores and releases calcium ions in muscle cells. It also helps in the breakdown of lipids.

Vacuoles in Plant and Animal Cells

A plant cell usually has one large central vacuole that stores water and cell sap and keeps the cell firm. Animal cells have several small vacuoles, if any, used mainly for temporary storage and transport. The plant vacuole is therefore much larger and more permanent.

When Lysosomal Enzymes Fail

Waste materials and worn-out parts would pile up inside the cell instead of being digested. The cell would become damaged and could die, and in the body this leads to storage diseases in which undigested substances accumulate in tissues.

Cristae and Cellular Respiration

Cristae are the folds of the inner membrane of the mitochondrion. They greatly increase the surface area available for the reactions of aerobic respiration, especially the electron transport chain, so more ATP can be produced.

Chromatin and Chromosomes

Chromatin is the loose, thread-like form of DNA and proteins found in the nucleus when the cell is not dividing. When the cell prepares to divide, chromatin condenses and coils into thick, visible structures called chromosomes. Chromosomes are therefore the condensed form of chromatin.

Parts of the Animal and Plant Cell: A Labelled Tour

Animal cell (left): 1 Mitochondrion; 2 Cell membrane; 3 Lysosome; 4 Endoplasmic reticulum; 5 Lysosome (small vesicle); 6 Golgi apparatus; 7 Vacuole (small). The large dark body in the centre is the nucleus. Plant cell (right): 1 Golgi apparatus; 2 Nucleus; 3 Endoplasmic reticulum; 4 Central vacuole; 5 Mitochondrion; 6 Mitochondrion (small body); 7 Chloroplast.

The thick outer boundary is the cell wall, and the green ovals are chloroplasts.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes
lessons.notes_html:
The Fluid Mosaic Model of the Cell Membrane

According to the fluid mosaic model, the cell membrane is a double layer of phospholipids in which proteins are embedded like pieces of a mosaic. The lipid layer is fluid, so the proteins can move sideways within it. Some proteins pass right through the membrane and act as channels or carriers, while others sit on the surface.

Cholesterol and carbohydrate chains are also present, and together they give a flexible, selectively permeable boundary.

Structure and Functions of the Cell Wall

The cell wall is a rigid layer outside the cell membrane, found in plant cells and made mainly of cellulose. It is freely permeable, so water and dissolved substances pass through it easily. It protects the cell, gives it a definite shape and prevents it from bursting when water enters.

In plant cells, neighbouring cells are connected through channels called plasmodesmata that pass through the wall.

Components of the Nucleus

The nucleus is bounded by a double nuclear membrane containing nuclear pores that control the passage of molecules. Inside is the nucleoplasm, a fluid containing chromatin, the DNA-protein material that carries hereditary information. The nucleolus is a dense region where ribosomes are assembled.

The nucleus controls all the activities of the cell and passes genetic information to the next generation.

Lysosome and Endoplasmic Reticulum

Lysosomes are small round sacs filled with digestive enzymes; they digest food particles, waste and worn-out organelles, acting as the cell's cleaning system. The endoplasmic reticulum is a network of folded membranes: the rough ER carries ribosomes and makes proteins, while the smooth ER makes lipids and detoxifies harmful substances. Both organelles work with the Golgi apparatus to process and transport cell products.

Formation and Function of the Golgi Complex

The Golgi complex is formed from stacks of flattened membrane sacs called cisternae, with vesicles budding from their edges. Proteins and lipids arriving from the endoplasmic reticulum enter on one side, are modified, sorted and packed into vesicles, and leave from the other side. These vesicles carry the products to the cell membrane for secretion or to other parts of the cell, and the Golgi also helps form lysosomes.

Structure and Functions of the Chloroplast

The chloroplast is a double-membraned organelle containing a fluid stroma and stacks of disc-like thylakoids called grana. The green pigment chlorophyll sits in the thylakoid membranes and captures light energy. In the thylakoids the light reactions of photosynthesis take place, while the dark reactions take place in the stroma, producing glucose.

Chloroplasts are therefore the sites of photosynthesis in plant cells.

lessons.title: Key Facts

Key Facts

  • Maximum growth of the cell occurs in the G1 phase of the cell cycle.
  • The chromosomes duplicate (DNA replicates) in the S phase of interphase.
  • It is NOT a characteristic of mitosis that the chromosome number is halved in daughter cells: mitosis occurs in somatic cells and produces two genetically identical daughter cells with the same chromosome number.
  • Chromosomes line up in the centre (equator) of the cell during metaphase of mitosis.
  • When the nuclear membrane is reforming around two sets of chromosomes, the cell is in telophase.
  • Meiosis-II is necessary after meiosis-I in order to separate the sister chromatids.

options: Four daughter cells with half the chromosome number

mcqs.why: During metaphase the chromosomes line up at the equator of the cell, attached to the spindle fibres.

lessons.title: Short Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Events of the G1 Phase

During G1 the cell grows rapidly, makes new proteins and organelles, and carries out its normal functions. It also prepares the materials needed for DNA replication in the next phase. The cell checks that conditions are suitable before it commits to dividing.

Purpose of the S Phase

In the S (synthesis) phase the cell copies its DNA, so that each chromosome comes to consist of two identical sister chromatids. This ensures that each daughter cell receives a complete copy of the genetic material after division.

Separation of Sister Chromatids

Sister chromatids separate during anaphase of mitosis. The spindle fibres pull them apart to opposite poles of the cell, so each pole receives an identical set of chromosomes.

Crossing Over and Genetic Variation

During prophase-I of meiosis, homologous chromosomes pair up and exchange segments of DNA, a process called crossing over. This creates new combinations of genes on the chromosomes, so the resulting gametes differ genetically from the parent and from each other.

Role of Spindle Fibres in Mitosis

Spindle fibres are made of microtubules and attach to the centromeres of chromosomes. During metaphase they line the chromosomes up at the equator, and during anaphase they pull the sister chromatids apart to opposite poles, ensuring an equal distribution of chromosomes.

Cytokinesis in Animal and Plant Cells

In animal cells cytokinesis takes place by a cleavage furrow: the cell membrane pinches inward until the cell divides into two. In plant cells a cell plate forms across the middle of the cell and grows outward to become the new cell wall and membranes, because the rigid wall prevents pinching.

Prophase of Mitosis and Prophase-I of Meiosis

In mitotic prophase, chromosomes condense, the nuclear membrane breaks down and the spindle forms, with no exchange of genetic material. In prophase-I of meiosis, homologous chromosomes pair up (synapsis) and crossing over takes place between them, and prophase-I is much longer, passing through leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene and diakinesis.

Meiosis and Mitosis: Chromosome Number

Mitosis produces two daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent (diploid stays diploid). Meiosis produces four daughter cells with half the chromosome number (diploid becomes haploid), because the chromosome number is halved in meiosis-I and the chromatids are then separated in meiosis-II.

Key Events of Anaphase

In anaphase the centromeres divide and the sister chromatids separate. Spindle fibres shorten and pull the chromatids, now called daughter chromosomes, to opposite poles of the cell. By the end of anaphase each pole has an identical set of chromosomes.

Function of the Centrosome

The centrosome is the microtubule-organising centre of the cell. During division it duplicates and its two copies move to opposite poles, where they organise the spindle fibres that move the chromosomes. In animal cells each centrosome contains a pair of centrioles.

Sister Chromatids and Their Separation in Meiosis

Sister chromatids are the two identical copies of a chromosome formed when DNA replicates in the S phase, joined at the centromere. In meiosis they stay together through meiosis-I and finally separate during anaphase-II of meiosis-II, so each gamete receives one chromatid.

Mitosis and Regeneration

Regeneration is the regrowth of lost or damaged body parts, and it depends on mitosis. Mitosis produces new, genetically identical cells that replace the lost cells and rebuild the tissue, as in the healing of a wound or the regrowth of a lizard's tail.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Events of the Phases of Mitosis

In prophase, chromosomes condense and become visible, the nuclear membrane breaks down and the spindle begins to form. In metaphase, chromosomes line up at the equator of the cell, attached to spindle fibres. In anaphase, sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles.

In telophase, nuclear membranes reform around the two sets of chromosomes and the chromosomes uncoil. Cytokinesis then divides the cytoplasm into two daughter cells.

Cytokinesis in Animal and Plant Cells

In animal cells, a ring of microfilaments beneath the membrane contracts and pinches the cell inward, forming a cleavage furrow that deepens until two daughter cells are produced. In plant cells, vesicles from the Golgi apparatus gather at the equator and fuse to form a cell plate, which grows outward until it joins the parent walls and becomes the new cell wall and membranes separating the two daughter cells.

Significance of Mitosis

Mitosis is essential for growth, because it increases the number of cells in a multicellular organism. It replaces worn-out and damaged cells, heals wounds and allows regeneration of lost parts. Because the daughter cells are genetically identical to the parent, mitosis maintains the chromosome number and passes the same hereditary information to every body cell.

Events of the Phases of Meiosis-I

In prophase-I, homologous chromosomes pair up and crossing over exchanges segments between them. In metaphase-I, the homologous pairs line up at the equator, with one homologue facing each pole. In anaphase-I, the homologous chromosomes separate and move to opposite poles, while sister chromatids stay together.

In telophase-I, the cell divides into two cells, each with half the chromosome number, and the chromosomes may partially uncoil.

Significance of Meiosis

Meiosis halves the chromosome number, so that when two gametes fuse at fertilisation the diploid number is restored. It produces genetic variation through crossing over and the independent assortment of chromosomes, which is the raw material for evolution. Meiosis also produces the gametes needed for sexual reproduction, giving offspring new combinations of characters.

lessons.notes_html:
Levels of Organisation: Cell to Organ System

The levels are: cell, tissue, organ, organ system and organism. Cells of the same type form a tissue, different tissues form an organ, organs working together form an organ system, and all the systems together make the organism.

Roles of the Epithelial Tissue of the Stomach

The epithelial tissue lines the inner wall of the stomach and protects it from the acid and enzymes of the gastric juice. Its cells secrete mucus, which coats and protects the wall, and they also produce pepsinogen and hydrochloric acid, which begin the digestion of proteins.

Smooth Muscles of the Stomach

The stomach wall has three layers of smooth muscle: outer longitudinal, middle circular and inner oblique. These muscles contract and relax in turn, churning the food and mixing it thoroughly with gastric juice, and they push the partially digested food onward into the small intestine.

Function of the Palisade Mesophyll

The palisade mesophyll is the upper layer of mesophyll tissue, made of tall, closely packed cells rich in chloroplasts. Because it lies just below the upper epidermis, it receives the most light and is the main site of photosynthesis in the leaf.

Pairs Compared: Tissue and Organ, Root and Shoot Systems, Leaf Tissues

Tissue and organ; ii. Root system and shoot system; iii. Epidermal and mesophyll tissue; iv.

Palisade and spongy mesophyll. i. A tissue is a group of similar cells performing one function, while an organ is made of several tissues working together for a larger function.

ii. The root system grows underground and absorbs water and salts, while the shoot system grows above ground and carries out photosynthesis and reproduction. iii.

Epidermal tissue is the protective outer layer of the leaf, while mesophyll tissue lies inside and carries out photosynthesis. iv. Palisade mesophyll consists of tall, tightly packed cells with many chloroplasts, while spongy mesophyll consists of loosely arranged cells with air spaces, which allow gas exchange.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Levels of Organisation in a Multicellular Organism

The cell is the basic unit of life and carries out all life processes. Similar cells form a tissue, such as muscle tissue, which performs one job better than a single cell could. Different tissues combine into an organ, such as the stomach, which performs a complete function.

Organs working together form an organ system, such as the digestive system, and all the systems together make the organism. Each level adds organisation, so the whole organism can carry out complex functions efficiently.

The Tissue Level: Plant and Animal Tissues

Explain plant and animal tissues. The tissue level is the level at which groups of similar cells work together for a common function. In plants the main tissues are meristematic tissue, which divides and produces new cells, and permanent tissues such as epidermis, parenchyma, xylem and phloem.

In animals the four main tissues are epithelial tissue (covering and lining), connective tissue (support and binding), muscle tissue (movement) and nervous tissue (control and coordination).

Tissue Composition of the Stomach

The stomach wall has four layers. The innermost epithelial tissue secretes mucus, pepsinogen and hydrochloric acid, protecting the wall and starting protein digestion. Beneath it, connective tissue supports the wall and carries blood vessels, nerves and lymphatics.

Three layers of smooth muscle churn the food and mix it with gastric juice. The outermost connective tissue encircles and supports the whole organ. Together these tissues let the stomach store, churn and chemically digest food.

Tissue Composition of the Leaf

The leaf is covered above and below by epidermal tissue, which protects it and controls water loss through stomata. Inside lies the mesophyll: the palisade layer, rich in chloroplasts, is the main photosynthetic tissue, while the spongy layer has air spaces for gas exchange. Vascular tissue runs through the veins: xylem brings water to the leaf cells, and phloem carries away the sugars made in photosynthesis.

Together these tissues let the leaf make food, exchange gases and transport materials.

Key Facts

  • Primarily, all enzymes are proteins.
  • An enzyme is best defined as a protein that speeds up chemical reactions.
  • Enzymes are specific in their action because their active sites fit specific substrates.

Metabolism: Catabolism and Anabolism

Anabolism is the building up of complex molecules from simpler ones, which needs energy, for example the synthesis of proteins from amino acids.

Anabolism: The Metabolism That Needs Energy

Give an example. Anabolism demands an input of energy, because small molecules are joined together to build larger ones. An example is photosynthesis, in which light energy is used to build glucose from carbon dioxide and water, or the synthesis of proteins from amino acids.

Enzymes and Their Role in Metabolism

An enzyme is a protein that acts as a biological catalyst: it speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up in it. In metabolism, enzymes lower the activation energy of reactions, so that the breakdown and building reactions of the cell take place fast enough to support life at body temperature.

The Active Site and Enzyme Specificity

Its shape and chemical nature match only a particular substrate, just as a lock fits one key, and this is why each enzyme acts on only one substrate or a small group of related substrates.

Characteristics of Enzymes

Enzymes are proteins that act as biological catalysts and are not used up in the reaction, so a small amount can catalyse many reactions. They are highly specific, each acting on a particular substrate because of the shape of its active site. They work best at an optimum temperature and pH, and are destroyed by extreme heat or pH.

They lower the activation energy of a reaction and speed it up, but do not change the products formed.

Factors Affecting Enzyme Activity

Temperature: activity rises with temperature up to an optimum (around body temperature in humans) and then falls sharply as the enzyme denatures. pH: each enzyme has an optimum pH, and strong acids or alkalis denature it. Substrate concentration: activity rises as more substrate is available, until all active sites are occupied.

Enzyme concentration, and the presence of activators, coenzymes or inhibitors, also change the rate of reaction.

Lock-and-Key and Induced Fit Models

In the Lock-and-Key model, proposed by Emil Fischer in 1894, the active site has a fixed, rigid shape and the substrate fits into it exactly like a key into a lock. In the Induced Fit model, proposed by Daniel Koshland in 1958, the active site is flexible: when the substrate enters, the active site changes shape slightly to fit it more closely, and this strain helps the reaction. The induced fit model explains why enzymes can act on slightly different substrates, which the rigid lock-and-key model cannot.

lessons.title: Short Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Importance of Oxidation–Reduction Reactions

Oxidation-reduction (redox) reactions transfer energy in living cells. When a molecule is oxidised it loses electrons and energy is released, and when another is reduced it gains those electrons. Photosynthesis and respiration are both redox processes, and they drive the formation and use of ATP, the cell's energy currency.

ATP and ADP in Cellular Metabolism

ATP is adenosine triphosphate and ADP is adenosine diphosphate. ATP stores energy in the bonds between its phosphate groups; when the last phosphate is removed, ATP becomes ADP and energy is released for cell work such as muscle contraction and active transport. ADP is then recharged to ATP using energy from respiration, so the ATP-ADP cycle powers metabolism.

Word Equation for Photosynthesis

Carbon dioxide + water, in the presence of light energy and chlorophyll, gives glucose + oxygen. In symbols: 6CO2 + 6H2O gives C6H12O6 + 6O2.

How Oxygen Is Produced in Photosynthesis

During the light reactions in the thylakoids, light energy splits water molecules, a process called photolysis. Water splits into hydrogen ions, electrons and oxygen gas. The oxygen is released into the air through the stomata, while the hydrogen and electrons are used to make ATP and NADPH for the dark reactions.

Organisms That Carry Out Photosynthesis

Photosynthesis is carried out by green plants, algae and some bacteria such as cyanobacteria. In plant cells the organelle responsible for absorbing light is the chloroplast, whose pigment chlorophyll in the thylakoid membranes captures light energy.

Main Purpose of Cellular Respiration

The main purpose of cellular respiration is to release the energy stored in food, especially glucose, and to transfer it into ATP. ATP then supplies energy for all the activities of the cell, such as movement, growth, active transport and the synthesis of new molecules.

Equation for Aerobic Respiration

Glucose + oxygen gives carbon dioxide + water + energy (ATP). In symbols: C6H12O6 + 6O2 gives 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy. The book's Figure 7.8 gives the total as 36 ATP from one glucose molecule in aerobic respiration.

Role of Oxygen in Aerobic Respiration

Oxygen acts as the final acceptor of electrons and hydrogen at the end of the electron transport chain. It combines with them to form water, which keeps the chain running and allows large amounts of ATP to be made. Without oxygen, the chain stops and the cell must rely on anaerobic respiration, which yields far less energy.

Aerobic and Anaerobic Respiration

Aerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose in the presence of oxygen, producing carbon dioxide, water and a large amount of energy (36 ATP per glucose in this book). Anaerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose without oxygen, producing much less energy, and in animals lactic acid, or in yeast ethanol and carbon dioxide, as by-products.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes
lessons.notes_html:
ATP: The Energy Currency of the Cell

ATP (adenosine triphosphate) consists of adenine, ribose sugar and three phosphate groups. Energy is stored in the bonds between the phosphate groups, especially the last one. When a cell needs energy, ATP is hydrolysed to ADP (adenosine diphosphate) and a phosphate, releasing energy for work such as contraction, transport and synthesis.

Because every cell makes ATP in respiration and spends it in the same way, ATP is called the energy currency of the cell.

The Process of Photosynthesis

Photosynthesis has two stages. In the light reactions, which take place in the thylakoids, chlorophyll absorbs light, water is split to release oxygen, and ATP and NADPH are formed. In the dark reactions (Calvin cycle), which take place in the stroma, carbon dioxide is fixed using the ATP and NADPH to build glucose.

Light energy is thus converted into chemical energy stored in food.

Intake of Carbon Dioxide and Water by Plants

Carbon dioxide enters the leaf from the air through the stomata, the small pores in the epidermis controlled by guard cells. Water is absorbed from the soil by root hairs and carried up through the xylem to the leaves. In the leaf, carbon dioxide and water meet in the chloroplasts, where they are used in photosynthesis to make glucose and release oxygen.

Types and Importance of Anaerobic Respiration

The two main types are lactic acid fermentation in animal muscle cells, which produces lactic acid and a little energy, and alcoholic fermentation in yeast and some bacteria, which produces ethanol and carbon dioxide. Anaerobic respiration is important because it lets cells make some ATP when oxygen is absent, for example during vigorous exercise, and it is used in industry for baking and brewing. Its drawback is the small energy yield and the harmful by-products.

Mechanism of Aerobic Respiration

Aerobic respiration has three main stages. In glycolysis in the cytoplasm, glucose is split into two molecules of pyruvic acid, giving a net gain of 2 ATP. Pyruvic acid enters the mitochondria, is converted to acetyl CoA, and passes through the Krebs cycle, releasing carbon dioxide and hydrogen carriers (NADH and FADH2).

In the electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane, these carriers release their energy to make most of the ATP, and oxygen accepts the final electrons to form water, giving 36 ATP in total in this book's account.

Transpiration and Its Types

Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the leaves. Its types are stomatal transpiration (through stomata, the main type), cuticular transpiration (through the cuticle of the leaf surface) and lenticular transpiration (through lenticels in stems).

Importance of the Transpirational Pull

As water evaporates from the leaves, a pull (tension) is created that draws water upward through the xylem from the roots. This transpirational pull is the main force lifting water and dissolved salts to the top of tall plants, without any expenditure of energy by the plant.

Transpiration: A Necessary Evil

No, transpiration is not harmful; it is a necessary evil with important benefits. It pulls water and minerals up from the roots, cools the leaves, and helps in the distribution of salts through the plant. Although it loses water, the plant gains far more from the upward transport and cooling it provides.

Pairs Compared: Xylem and Phloem, Transpiration and Guttation, Plant Groups, Types of Transpiration

Xylem and phloem; ii. Transpiration and guttation; iii. Hydrophytes and halophytes; iv.

Hydrophytes and xerophytes; v. Lenticular transpiration and stomatal transpiration. i.

Xylem transports water and salts upward and is made of dead cells, while phloem transports food in both directions and is made of living cells. ii. Transpiration is the loss of water as vapour, while guttation is the loss of liquid water as droplets from leaf margins.

iii. Hydrophytes live in water, while halophytes live in salty habitats and tolerate salt. iv.

Hydrophytes live in water with abundant supply, while xerophytes live in dry deserts and conserve water. v. Lenticular transpiration takes place through lenticels in stems, while stomatal transpiration takes place through stomata in leaves.

Opening and Closing of Stomata

Stomata are pores bounded by two guard cells. When guard cells take in water by osmosis they become turgid and bow outward, opening the pore. When they lose water they become flaccid and close together, shutting the pore.

Light, potassium ion movement and the water supply of the leaf control this turgor change, so stomata open in daylight for photosynthesis and gas exchange, and close to reduce water loss.

Internal Structure of the Root and Uptake of Water and Salts

The root in cross-section has an outer epidermis with root hairs, a cortex of parenchyma cells, an endodermis, and a central vascular cylinder containing xylem and phloem. Water enters root hairs by osmosis, because the cell sap is more concentrated than the soil solution, and passes through the cortex to the xylem. Salts are taken up mainly by active transport, using energy, and then move with the water into the xylem for transport upward.

Mechanism of Transport of Water and Salts

Water is absorbed by root hairs by osmosis and moves through the cortex into the xylem vessels. It then rises through the xylem by the combined forces of root pressure, capillary action, cohesion between water molecules and adhesion to vessel walls, and above all the transpirational pull from the leaves. Salts move with the water, having been taken up by the roots by active transport, and are distributed to all parts of the plant.

Food Translocation: The Pressure Flow Mechanism

In the pressure flow mechanism, sugars made in the leaves (the source) are actively loaded into the phloem sieve tubes. Water follows by osmosis, raising the pressure at the source end. At the sink (roots, fruits or growing parts), sugars are removed for use or storage, water leaves the phloem, and the pressure falls.

This pressure difference pushes the sugary sap from source to sink through the phloem.

Osmotic Adjustments in Hydrophytes, Xerophytes and Halophytes

Hydrophytes live in water, so they face no shortage: they have broad floating leaves with many stomata on the upper surface, and water moves out freely (the water lily is the book's example). Xerophytes live in deserts: they have deep roots, very few stomata and a thick waxy cuticle to cut water loss, and some, like cacti, store water in soft, juicy succulent stems or roots. Halophytes live in salty water: water tends to leave their bodies, so they absorb salts to make their cells hypertonic, and excrete excess salt through salt glands on their leaves; many sea grasses belong to this group.

lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
Key Facts

  • Bacteria commonly reproduce by binary fission.
  • The primary method of reproduction in yeast is budding.
  • During harsh conditions, some bacteria form thick-walled endospores that survive until conditions improve.
  • An example of vegetative propagation through runners is the strawberry.
  • The plant that propagates through tubers is the potato.
  • The flower does NOT help a plant in vegetative propagation — rhizomes, corms and runners do, but the flower is the organ of sexual reproduction.
  • The filament is NOT a part of the carpel: the carpel consists of stigma, style and ovary, while the filament is part of the stamen.
  • The structure that forms (contains) the female gametophyte in flowering plants is the ovule, inside which the embryo sac develops.
  • The male gametophyte in flowering plants is the pollen grain.
  • In the life cycle of flowering plants, the structure that is triploid (3n) is the endosperm nucleus, formed by the fusion of a sperm with the diploid fusion nucleus.
  • Double fertilisation involves the fertilisation of the egg and of the fusion nucleus by the two sperms (male gametes) of the same pollen grain.

mcqs.why: Bacteria commonly reproduce by binary fission, dividing one cell into two genetically identical cells.

mcqs.why: A potato tuber is an underground stem swollen with stored food; its buds (eyes) sprout into new plants.

mcqs.why: The carpel consists of stigma, style and ovary; the filament is part of the stamen, the male part of the flower.

mcqs.why: The structure that contains the female gametophyte is the ovule, inside which the embryo sac develops.

mcqs.why: The male gametophyte is the pollen grain, while the female gametophyte is the embryo sac inside the ovule.

lessons.title: Short Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Budding in Yeast

In budding, a small outgrowth (bud) appears on the yeast cell and grows, while the nucleus divides and one daughter nucleus moves into the bud. The bud then separates from the parent cell and grows into a new yeast cell. Sometimes buds remain attached for a while, forming a chain of cells.

Spore Formation in Fungi

In fungi such as Rhizopus, spores are produced in sac-like sporangia at the tips of aerial hyphae. When the sporangium bursts, the light spores are scattered by wind. Each spore that lands in suitable conditions germinates and grows into a new fungal body.

Advantages of Spore Formation

Spores are light and easily dispersed by wind and water, so the organism spreads to new places. In bacteria, thick-walled endospores survive harsh conditions such as heat, dryness and lack of food, and germinate when conditions improve. Spore formation therefore aids both dispersal and survival.

Vegetative Propagation Through Runners

Runners (stolons) are horizontal stems that grow along the surface of the ground from the parent plant. At their nodes they produce roots and new shoots, which grow into independent plants. Strawberry is the common example: one parent plant can thus produce many new plants around itself.

Potato Reproduction Through Tubers

A potato tuber is an underground stem swollen with stored food, bearing buds in its eyes. When a tuber, or a piece of it with an eye, is planted, the buds sprout into new shoots and roots, and a new potato plant grows. The new plant is genetically identical to the parent.

Advantages and Disadvantages of Vegetative Propagation

Advantages: new plants are identical to the parent, so good characters are preserved; it is fast, and plants that do not produce seeds can still be multiplied. Disadvantages: there is no genetic variation, so all the plants are equally vulnerable to disease and changing conditions, and diseases of the parent are passed on to the offspring.

The Four Whorls of a Flower

The four whorls are: calyx, made of sepals, which protect the bud; corolla, made of petals, which attract pollinators; androecium, the male whorl, made of stamens, each with a filament and an anther; and gynoecium, the female whorl, made of carpels, each with a stigma, style and ovary.

Formation of the Egg Cell and Polar Nuclei

Inside the ovule, a megaspore mother cell divides by meiosis to form four megaspores, of which one survives. Its nucleus divides three times by mitosis to form eight nuclei in the embryo sac. These organise into an egg cell with two synergids at one end, three antipodal cells at the other, and two polar nuclei in the centre, which fuse to form the diploid fusion nucleus.

Pairs Compared: Modes of Reproduction and Flower Parts

Asexual and sexual reproduction; ii. Binary fission in bacteria and amoeba; iii. Stolon and rhizome; iv.

Bulb and corm; v. Cutting and grafting; vi. Vegetative propagation and artificial propagation; vii.

Male and female gametophytes; viii. Calyx and corolla; ix. Stamen and carpel.

i. Asexual reproduction uses one parent and produces identical offspring without gametes, while sexual reproduction uses two parents and gametes, producing varied offspring. ii.

In bacteria, binary fission is division of a single cell into two identical cells, while in Amoeba the same process is a form of asexual reproduction in a unicellular animal. iii. A stolon (runner) grows above the ground, while a rhizome is an underground horizontal stem.

iv. A bulb is a short stem with fleshy leaves (onion), while a corm is a solid swollen stem base (gladiolus). v.

In cutting, a piece of stem or leaf is planted to grow a new plant, while in grafting a scion is joined onto a rootstock. vi. Vegetative propagation is natural reproduction from plant parts, while artificial propagation is the same process carried out deliberately by humans.

vii. The male gametophyte is the pollen grain, while the female gametophyte is the embryo sac. viii.

The calyx is the whorl of sepals, while the corolla is the whorl of petals. ix. The stamen is the male part (filament + anther), while the carpel is the female part (stigma + style + ovary).

Parts of a Flower: A Labelled Tour

From the top downward, the labelled parts are: petal; anther (the pollen-bearing head of the stamen); filament (the stalk of the stamen); stigma (the receptive tip of the carpel); style (the stalk of the carpel); ovary (the swollen base of the carpel containing ovules); ovule (inside the ovary); sepal (the green leaf-like part below the petals); receptacle (the base on which the flower parts sit); and pedicel (the stalk of the flower).

lessons.title: Detailed Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Binary Fission in Bacteria

In binary fission, the single circular DNA of the bacterium first replicates, and the two copies move to opposite ends of the cell. A cross-wall (septum) then grows inward across the middle of the cell, and the cell membrane and wall divide. The result is two genetically identical daughter bacteria, each with its own copy of DNA, and under favourable conditions this can repeat every 20 minutes or so.

Vegetative Propagation and Its Modified Structures

Differentiate among different plant structures modified for vegetative propagation. Vegetative propagation is asexual reproduction in which a new plant grows from a vegetative part of the parent, such as a stem, root or leaf, without seeds. Modified stems include runners (strawberry, above ground), rhizomes (ginger, underground), tubers (potato, swollen underground stem), bulbs (onion, fleshy leaves on a short stem) and corms (solid underground stem bases).

Roots and leaves can also produce new plants in some species, and all the offspring are genetically identical to the parent.

Artificial Propagation by Humans

Humans use cuttings, in which a piece of stem, root or leaf is cut and planted until it roots. In layering, a branch is bent to the ground and covered with soil until it roots, then separated. In grafting, a scion (shoot) of a desired variety is joined to the rootstock of another plant so they grow as one.

Tissue culture grows many plantlets from a small piece of tissue in a laboratory medium. All these methods preserve the parent's characters exactly.

Sporophyte and Gametophyte

State their roles in the life cycle of plants. The sporophyte is the diploid (2n) generation that produces spores by meiosis in sporangia. The gametophyte is the haploid (n) generation that grows from a spore and produces gametes by mitosis.

In the plant life cycle these two generations alternate: the sporophyte gives rise to the gametophyte through spores, and the gametophyte gives rise to the next sporophyte when gametes fuse at fertilisation.

Life Cycle of Flowering Plants

The flowering plant itself is the diploid sporophyte. In its flowers, meiosis produces haploid spores: microspores in the anthers and megaspores in the ovules. These grow into the gametophytes: the pollen grain (male) and the embryo sac (female).

The pollen grain produces two male gametes, and the embryo sac contains the egg. At double fertilisation, one sperm fuses with the egg to form the diploid zygote, which grows into the new sporophyte embryo, while the other fuses with the fusion nucleus to form the triploid endosperm that feeds it.

Development of the Female Gametophyte (Embryo Sac)

Within the ovule, a diploid megaspore mother cell divides by meiosis into four haploid megaspores, three of which degenerate and one survives. The surviving megaspore's nucleus divides three times by mitosis, producing eight nuclei. These organise into the seven-celled embryo sac: an egg cell and two synergids at the micropylar end, three antipodal cells at the opposite end, and two polar nuclei in the centre.

This embryo sac is the female gametophyte, ready for fertilisation.

The single circular DNA of the bacterium replicates

mcqs.why: In 1 hour there are 60 ÷ 20 = 3 rounds of division, and the number doubles each round: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8, so 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 bacteria.
